026.subtitle: The chariot called King of Wheels

commentary.meaning: The march begins. Two names, each filling a whole line, and both built on the same middle element — rathārūḍha, mounted on the chariot — so that the couplet moves like a column with a drum in it. The first seats her on the Cakrarāja, the King of Wheels, and says nothing whatever about how the vehicle looks; what it reports is that every weapon there is has been loaded onto it and that she rides fitted out with all of them. The second names a second chariot, the Geyacakra or Wheel of Song, and the person on it: Mantriṇī, her minister, who keeps station beside her and attends her throughout. Two chariots, two kinds of power — arms in the first line and counsel in the second — and with that the stotra has moved, without announcing the change, from describing a body to describing an order of battle. From here to the eighty-fourth name the subject is the war.
commentary.history:
The Lalitopākhyāna does not tell the campaign against Bhaṇḍāsura as a myth. It tells it as a war book, in the manner of the Mahābhārata: named commanders, armies counted in akṣauhiṇīs, a chain of command, several days of fighting with a pause at nightfall, and vehicles assigned strictly by rank. Three chariots leave Śrīpura, and the purāṇa has already placed them in the city before the campaign starts, drawn up in the grounds of the Cintāmaṇi mansion — the Cakrarāja in the lotus grove to the south-west, the Geyacakra to the north-west, the Kiricakra of the next verse to the north-east.

The Cakrarāja is hers, and it is described as enormous and as having nine tiers or steps. The tradition takes those nine tiers to be the nine enclosures of the Śrīcakra, which is a reading the words invite rather than resist: cakrarāja is one of the ordinary names of the Śrīcakra itself. So cakrarāja-ratha says in two words that she goes to war seated inside her own diagram, and that the diagram is not a picture of a place but a vehicle that moves. Each tier of it is occupied. The purāṇa spends chapters stationing deities on the steps, so that when the stotra says sarvāyudha, all the weapons, it is not reaching for a superlative. On this chariot the armament is the personnel: the weapons are goddesses, and the goddesses are the enclosures of the yantra.

The Geyacakra belongs to Mantriṇī and has seven steps, and the purāṇa's roster for it is worth knowing because it shows what kind of army this is. On the first step Mantriṇī herself with Saṅgītayoginī; on the second Rati, Prīti and Manojā with lutes; on the third the five goddesses of Kāma's arrows — Drāviṇī, Śoṣiṇī, Bandhinī, Mohinī and Unmādinī — with five forms of the love-god beneath them; on the fourth the eight mother-powers headed by Brāhmī, and below them Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti, Kīrti, Śānti, Puṣṭi and Tuṣṭi; on the fifth sixteen goddesses headed by Vāmā; on the sixth the eight Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga; on the seventh Mātaṅgī, Siddhalakṣmī and the powers of the guardians of the quarters. An army made of music, desire, speech and prosperity is going to war, and the chariot it rides in is called the Wheel of Song.

Mantriṇī is the second figure of the tradition after Lalitā. Her other names are Śyāmalā, Rājaśyāmalā and Mātaṅgī; she is dark, she carries a vīṇā, and she governs speech, music and counsel. Mantriṇī is simply the feminine of mantrin, the king's minister, and in the ritual system of Śrīvidyā she and Daṇḍinī are worshipped as the two officers of state. Agastya, in the frame narrative that opens this text, complains that Hayagrīva has already given him the thousand names of Mantriṇī and of Daṇḍinī and has withheld only Lalitā's — which tells you that both had thousand-name hymns of their own, and that a listener in the eighth or tenth century would have heard geyacakra-rathārūḍha-mantriṇī and pictured a specific goddess with a specific instrument, not an allegory of good advice.

What the sahasranāma does with all this is compression. The purāṇa needs several chapters to load the chariots; the hymn needs thirty-two syllables. This is worth holding on to for the next eight verses, which can read like a catalogue of proper names if you do not know that each one is a compressed chapter. The Vāgdevatās are not summarising the story for someone who has not heard it. They are giving the reciter a set of handles.
commentary.practice:
The two lines of this verse are metrical twins, and hearing the twinning is most of the work. Each is a single sixteen-syllable name; each has -rathārūḍha- sitting in exactly the same position, as its fifth to twelfth syllables; each ends in a past participle in -ā. Chant it once slowly with that shape in mind and the verse stops being two mouthfuls and becomes a couplet with a refrain in the middle.

The sound to isolate first is ḍh in ārūḍha, the voiced retroflex aspirate. Curl the tongue-tip back, keep the voice on, and let a distinct puff of breath out as the tongue comes away. It occurs twice in this verse and twice more in the next, so it is worth the drill. Then pariṣkṛtā, which packs three difficulties into four syllables: the retroflex ṣ, the cluster ṣk, and the syllabic ṛ. Take it as pa-riṣ-kṛ-tā, keeping the ṛ short — it is one beat and no more.

That word also sets up the single best drill in this stretch of the stotra, and the answer arrives in the very next verse. This verse ends in pariṣkṛtā with a retroflex ṣ; the next ends in puraskṛtā with a plain dental s. The two words are near-identical in shape, they are both built on √kṛ, and they rhyme across the join between the verses. The retroflex in pariṣkṛtā is not arbitrary: an s following the i of pari- is turned retroflex by rule, while the s of puras- is protected by the a in front of it. Say the two words back to back until the difference is audible, because the same rule will govern half the retroflex sibilants you meet from here on.

Mantriṇī is three difficulties in a row as well. The cluster ntr is dental n, dental t, then r, all in one release; the ṇ that follows is retroflex; and the final ī is long. Immediately after it comes parisevitā, which is dental all the way through. So the word pair mantriṇī-parisevitā takes the tongue-tip back and then forward four times in eight syllables. Go slowly.

Two sandhis are hidden in the writing. Sarva plus āyudha has given sarvāyudha, and ratha plus ārūḍha has given rathārūḍha; in both cases two a-sounds have merged into a single long ā written with one mātrā, so the ear gets no warning of where the seam is. Notice also that geya is two syllables, ge-ya, with a pure long e — never the diphthong an English speaker will want to put there.

The metrical caesura falls after the eighth syllable of each line, which in both cases lands inside a word: cakrarājarathā | rūḍha and geyacakrarathā | rūḍha. Hear the division without opening a gap in the sound. Most reciters take the actual breath at the end of the first line and run each name through in one arc.

As for what to hold: this is the point where the stotra stops looking at her and starts following her. The verse has no adjective of beauty in it. It reports equipment and it reports a subordinate keeping station, and the change of register after twenty-five verses of ornament is itself the thing to notice.

027.subtitle: The boar-wheel chariot and the wall of fire

commentary.meaning: The third chariot and the shape of the field. Daṇḍanāthā — the mistress of the rod, the punitive arm of the goddess's government — rides the Kiricakra, the Boar Wheel, and she is puraskṛtā, placed in front: she has the advance, and the road is cleared where she goes. Then the second name pulls the eye back from the point of the column to the perimeter of the whole army. Jvālāmālinī has thrown up a rampart of fire around the encampment, and the goddess is described as moving in the middle of it. The two names point in opposite directions, one forward along the line of march and one outward to the edge of the position, and between them they describe a formation rather than a person. Note also which verb is used of her: not standing, not seated, but ga, going. Inside a ring of fire a hundred yojanas across, she is the one thing in motion.
commentary.history:
Kiri is a hog, and the chariot is the Boar Wheel because the goddess who rides it is boar-faced. Daṇḍanāthā has as many names as Mantriṇī: Vārāhī, Daṇḍinī, Potriṇī, Daṇḍanāyikā. She is the commander of the forces where Mantriṇī is the minister, and the difference is exact. A mantrin advises; a daṇḍanātha holds the daṇḍa, the rod, which in Sanskrit political vocabulary is the whole apparatus of coercion — punishment, police, the army, the king's power to compel. Kauṭilya's science of government is called daṇḍanīti, the handling of the rod. To say that the mistress of the rod goes in front of the goddess is to describe a state on the march, not a divine escort.

Her chariot has five tiers to Mantriṇī's seven and Lalitā's nine, and the purāṇa's roster for it is a good deal grimmer than the roster for the Wheel of Song. Below Daṇḍanāthā stand Jṛmbhiṇī, Mohinī and Stambhinī — the powers of yawning, bewilderment and paralysis — carrying a pestle, a plough and a vessel of liquor. Further down are the seven Dhātunāthās, the mistresses of the bodily constituents, with names of the Ḍākinī type; a lion called Caṇḍocchaṇḍa stands before the chariot; and there is a rank of eight headed by Vārtālī, one of Vārāhī's own names. The plough and the pestle are the weapons of Balarāma, farm implements used as clubs, and they suit her: this is the ugly end of the operation. In the Śrīcakra worship she is stationed in one of the outer enclosures, on the perimeter, which is where a commander of forces belongs.

Jvālāmālinī, the second half of the verse, is one of the fifteen Nityā goddesses, the eternal ones who will be named in the next verse. Her name means garlanded with flame, and at Lalitā's order she made the encampment a fortress. The purāṇa gives its dimensions in the way purāṇas do — a wall of fire some thirty yojanas high and a hundred across, with a single gap left open at the southern end, a yojana wide, facing Śūnyaka, so that the army could sortie. Whatever one makes of the arithmetic, the detail about the gap is not decoration. It is load-bearing for the next four verses. The fire-fort is a closed space with one door, and the entire crisis that follows happens inside it: Viśukra will creep up to the wall in the dark and throw his obstruction-engine over it, the paralysis will spread within an enclosure nobody can leave, and Gaṇeśa when he is born will have to search the enclosure to find where the thing landed.

Prākāra is the specific word for the rampart of a fortified town — the dictionary defines it as a wall raised on a mound of earth. So the besieging army has built itself a city wall out of fire, facing the demon's city across the plain. Śūnyaka, whose name means the empty place, will be reduced by a weapon to exactly what its name says; her own city, meanwhile, is made of nothing but burning. The two fortifications are set against each other deliberately.

One small point of vocabulary. The stotra calls her Jvālāmālinikā, with a -ka suffix on the end, and not Jvālāmālinī. The suffix is affectionate or diminutive in ordinary Sanskrit and is often added simply to make a name fit a line, and here it does both jobs at once: it fills the metre and it makes the fiercest goddess in the sentence sound, for one syllable, like somebody's daughter.
commentary.practice:
This verse ends in puraskṛtā and the last one ended in pariṣkṛtā. Chant them one after the other. Both are past participles of √kṛ with a prefix; the first has the retroflex ṣ because the s has been retroflexed by the i of pari- in front of it, and the second keeps a plain dental s because the a of puras- protects it. Pa-riṣ-kṛ-tā, pu-ras-kṛ-tā. That contrast is the most compact retroflex drill anywhere in the first fifty verses, and if you can hear it you can hear the difference everywhere else.

Daṇḍanāthā is the same lesson inside a single word. It begins with the retroflex pair ṇḍ — tongue-tip curled back for both consonants with no forward movement between them — and then goes immediately to a dental n and an aspirated dental th. Da-ṇḍa-nā-thā: back, back, forward, forward, with a puff of breath on the last. The th is t plus aspiration and never the sound in English "thin".

Kiri is easy to get wrong because it is so short. Two light syllables, both with a short i, and no stress on either; the temptation is to lengthen the first because the words around it are long. Then jvālāmālinikākṣipta, which is the hardest single stretch in the verse. It opens with jv, a cluster English does not have — say the j fully and let the v follow inside the same release, not as a separate syllable. It runs four long ā's in a row. And it ends with the seam where mālinikā meets ākṣipta: two long ā's swallowing each other into one, followed at once by kṣ. Break it as jvā-lā-mā-li-nī-kā | ā-kṣip-ta, rebuild it, and only then take it at speed.

Prākāra wants care in the opposite direction: two long ā's and an unaspirated k in the middle, with no breath after it. Vahni is v then h then n, three separate sounds. And madhyagā ends the line on dhy, an aspirated dental d immediately followed by y, which most learners simplify to a j-like sound.

The second line is a single sixteen-syllable name with no natural joint at the eighth syllable — the caesura lands inside -kākṣipta-, at the worst possible place. Most reciters take a light breath after jvālāmālinikākṣipta, which is one syllable late but divides the compound where it actually divides, between the thrower and the thing thrown.

On what to hold: the verse asks you to see two things at once, the point of the spear and the ring around the camp. It is worth noticing that the goddess is placed at neither. She is between them, in the middle, and the word for what she is doing there is simply going.

commentary.meaning: Two names about her face while she watches. Neither reports a blow struck by her. The first says she was gladdened by the valour of the śaktis who had set themselves to destroy Bhaṇḍa's army; the second that she was leaning forward, eager, to see the swelling force with which the Nityās fought. Harṣitā and samutsukā are both words for a spectator, and the second of them, samutsuka, is the word for somebody who cannot sit still. The verse could have said that she killed them. It says instead that she enjoyed watching, and the whole of the next three verses will keep saying it — delighted, delighted, pleased, overjoyed. Since every one of these fighters is her own emanation, the pleasure being described is a strange one. She is watching herself fight, and taking a spectator's pleasure in it, which is exactly what the tradition means when it says the world is her play.
commentary.history:
The army in this war is unusual in that it contains almost no gods. In the Lalitopākhyāna the Śaktisenā is created by Lalitā herself out of herself, and apart from Kāmeśvara the devas are not in the line of battle at all — they are the reason for the war and its beneficiaries, but they do not fight it. This is the opposite of the arrangement in the Devī Māhātmya, where the mother-powers step out of the bodies of Brahmā, Śiva, Skanda, Viṣṇu and Indra and go into battle wearing each god's shape, ornaments and mount. There the goddess is assembled out of the gods; here the goddess assembles the fighters out of herself. The two verses quoted below sit on either side of that difference and are worth reading in that order.

The Nityās named in the second half are the fifteen eternal goddesses of her retinue, and the tradition associates them one to one with the fifteen lunar days of the bright fortnight: Kāmeśvarī, Bhagamālinī, Nityaklinnā, Bheruṇḍā, Vahnivāsinī, Mahāvajreśvarī, Śivadūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī, Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, Sarvamaṅgalā, Jvālāmālinī and Citrā, with Lalitā herself counted as the sixteenth and the full moon. Jvālāmālinī, who built the wall of fire in the verse just past, is the fourteenth of them, so the two verses are linked by more than sequence. It is also worth registering what it means to send the tithi-goddesses into a battle. The days of the waxing moon are attacking, in order, and the demon is being worn down by the calendar.

Āṭopa, the word chosen for the manner of their attack, is a small masterpiece of tone. Monier-Williams gives it as puffing, swelling, then a multitude, then flatulence, then pride and self-conceit. It is not a dignified word. It is the swagger of troops who know they are winning, the visible inflation of confidence, and the poet has used it of the Nityās while the goddess watches from the chariot with obvious enjoyment. Set beside the grim inventory of the Boar Wheel in the previous verse, it shows how wide the emotional range of this section is: the same campaign contains paralysis-goddesses with pestles and a mother delighting in her daughters' swank.

The grammar of both names puts her in the receiving position. Harṣitā and, in the next verses, nanditā, toṣitā and praharṣitā are all causative participles: she is made glad, she is caused to rejoice, the pleasure is done to her by what she sees. For a hymn otherwise composed of a thousand assertions of sovereignty, this is a notable stretch of passives. Whatever the theology says about her being the only agent in the universe, the poetry has her sitting in a chariot being delighted by other people.

A note on the enemy's scale, since the stotra gives none. The purāṇa's numbers for Bhaṇḍa's forces run to thousands of akṣauhiṇīs and forty named generals, and the fighting is organised into days with commanders killed in a definite order — the sons, then the brothers, then the demon himself. The stotra tracks that order exactly over the next five verses. If the sequence of these names has ever seemed arbitrary, it is not: it is a casualty list in chronological order.
commentary.practice:
The verse is two more sixteen-syllable names, one to a line, and both are long tatpuruṣa chains that end in a participle. The trick with a name of this shape is to find the joint. In the first line the joint is after -vadhodyukta-: everything before it describes what the śaktis were bent on doing, everything after it is their valour and her pleasure in it. In the second the joint is after -āṭopa-. Breathe with those joints in mind and the lines organise themselves.

Bhaṇḍa is aspirated bh followed by the retroflex pair ṇḍ, and it recurs in three of the next four verses, so fix it now. The bh is a b with an audible puff of breath, not a v and not an f; the ṇḍ is made with the tongue-tip curled back for both consonants together.

Vadhodyukta hides a sandhi that the writing conceals: vadha plus udyukta, a short a and a short u merging into a single o. Knowing that keeps the sense visible while you chant — the slaughter, then the being-braced-for. The cluster dy in the middle is a dental d immediately followed by y, and the two must be heard as two.

Harṣitā gives you ṣ after r, which is the ordinary Sanskrit outcome and worth noticing as a pattern rather than a fact about this word: r pulls the following sibilant back into the retroflex position. The same thing has happened in varṣiṇī three verses later.

The second line is a chain of long ā's across two sandhi seams. Nityā plus parākrama plus āṭopa gives nityāparākramāṭopa, and the ā's of -krama and āṭopa have fused into one. Note that the ṭ of āṭopa is retroflex; so is the ṇ of nirīkṣaṇa a few syllables later, and there the retroflexion is caused by the ṛ and the kṣ in front of it — the same rule that will give you prāṇa and haraṇa in the verse after next. Kṣ itself is k plus the retroflex ṣ, never an English "x".

Samutsukā ends the verse on ts, which is a genuine cluster of two dental sounds and not the ch of English "church". Sa-mut-su-kā, with the t released before the s begins.

On what to hold while chanting: the verse is an instruction in how to watch. The traditional reading is that everything in the field of experience is her power in action, and that the appropriate attitude toward it is neither anxiety nor detachment but this — leaning forward, keenly interested, delighted by the courage of what is not, in the end, anybody else.

029.subtitle: The nine-year-old and the thirty princes

commentary.meaning: Two more names of pleasure, and this time the pleasure is a mother's twice over. Bhaṇḍa sent his thirty sons into the field; Bālā, who has the appearance of a nine-year-old girl and is the goddess's own daughter, went out against them, and her daring gave Lalitā open joy — nanditā, made to rejoice. Then Mantriṇī, whom the verse calls ambā, mother, brought down Viṣaṅga, one of the demon's two brothers, and that satisfied her: toṣitā. Both names are assembled the same way, deed first, doer second, and then a single word for the feeling produced in the one who is watching. What repays attention is who does the killing. In the first half a child, in the second a minister, and in neither the sovereign. The stotra is four names into the war and the goddess has not yet lifted a hand.
commentary.history:
Bhaṇḍa had thirty sons and the purāṇa names every one of them — Caturbāhu, Cakorākṣa, Catuḥśiras, Vajraghoṣa, Ūrdhvakeśa, Mahākāya, Mahāhanu, Makhaśatru, Makhaskandin, Siṃhaghoṣa and so on down to Atimāya, Bṛhanmāya and Upamāya at the end of the list. The names are a fair sample of the whole demon roster: several of them mean enemy of sacrifice, several are compounded with māyā, illusion, and several are simply large. They had trampled Indra and Varuṇa, their father told them, and this women's army would be no trouble at all.

Bālā is introduced at that point and the description is careful. She looks exactly like Lalitā, she is perpetually nine years old, she is a mine of every branch of learning, her body has the colour of the rising sun and the slenderness of a creeper, and she is always to be found at the footstool of the great queen. Then two phrases that are hard to improve on: she is the goddess's own vital breath walking about outside her, and she is her fourth eye. When Bālā decides she will kill the demon's sons and comes to ask permission, her mother refuses, and the refusal is the least theological speech in the whole work. Your limbs are soft, you are only nine, this is your first action, your training is barely finished, you are my only daughter, and without you my breathing does not continue even for a moment. We have Daṇḍinī and Mantriṇī and crores of śaktis to do the fighting. Why would you do this foolish thing. Bālā insists; her mother gives in, embraces her, takes off her own armour and puts it on her; and Bālā goes out and takes the heads off all thirty with thirty crescent-tipped arrows.

That girl is not only a character in a story. In Śrīvidyā practice Bālā is the deity of a three-syllable mantra, and it is very often the first mantra a student is given, years before the fifteen-syllabled one. The three syllables in question are aiṃ, klīṃ and sauḥ — which are precisely the three that the nyāsa preceding this stotra places on the reciter's fingers and on six points of the body before a word of the hymn is spoken. The tradition also reads those three as the seed, the power and the pin of the pañcadaśākṣarī, and both readings are current; what matters here is that a reciter who has done the nyāsa has already put the child-goddess on his own hands before arriving at name 74. The stotra will come back to her much later and simply call her Bālā, at name 965, followed at once by līlāvinodinī, she who is amused by play.

The second half of the verse raises a genuine problem that the tradition has never resolved. Viṣaṅga and Viśukra are Bhaṇḍa's brothers, born, in the purāṇa's account, out of what was left of the same heap of ash from which he himself was shaped. In the narrative chapters it is Śyāmalā — Mantriṇī — who fights Viśukra and shatters him with the missile called Brahmaśiras, and Daṇḍanāthā who kills Viṣaṅga with her plough and pestle. This verse and the next assign it the other way round: Mantriṇī kills Viṣaṅga, and Vārāhī takes the life of Viśukra. The two accounts sit a few chapters apart in the same book. Translators and commentators have noticed and have not agreed on what to do about it, and it is a useful thing to have seen once, because it shows that the hymn and the narrative it is embedded in were not composed as a single piece by a single hand.

The order of events is also not the story's order. In the purāṇa the sons die, then Viśukra throws his obstruction-engine and Gaṇeśa is born to destroy it, and only after that do the two brothers fall. The stotra puts both brothers before Gaṇeśa. It has grouped the deaths by kind rather than by day.
commentary.practice:
The one thing to get right in this verse is the word mantriṇyambā, which is where the second line begins. It is mantriṇī plus ambā, and the long ī of mantriṇī has been turned into the semivowel y in front of the following vowel — the change the grammarians call yaṇ. What you see written is मन्त्रिण्यम्बा, with the conjunct ण्य carrying the whole transformation, and what you say is man-tri-ṇyam-bā, four syllables where the two words apart would have given five. This is one of the commonest sandhis in the stotra and one of the hardest to spot, because the vowel that has vanished leaves no trace at all. The other direction is easier to remember than the rule: whenever you meet a ण्य or a त्य or a व्य in the middle of a compound and the sense will not come, try putting a long ī or a short i back in.

The verse is also a clean drill in the difference between dental n and retroflex ṇ, because the first line has both in quantity. Bhaṇḍa takes the retroflex — tongue-tip curled back through the whole ṇḍ — while bālā, vikrama and nanditā are entirely dental, and nanditā has two dental n sounds in four syllables. Chant bhaṇḍaputravadhodyukta as one unit and bālāvikramananditā as another, and let the tongue reset between them.

Viṣaṅga is worth taking apart because its neighbour in the next verse is nearly its twin. Vi-ṣaṅ-ga: retroflex ṣ, then the guttural nasal ṅ made at exactly the place where the following g is made, so the tongue does not travel. In the next verse comes Viśukra, with the palatal ś. The two brothers of the demon are distinguished, in sound, by a single sibilant moved one place forward in the mouth. Say viṣaṅga and viśukra one after the other until they are two different words.

Toṣitā has a retroflex ṣ of a different origin from harṣitā's in the verse before. There the r pulled the sibilant back; here the ṣ belongs to the root √tuṣ itself and has been there all along. The audible result is the same; knowing which is which keeps you from over-applying the rule.

Vadhodyukta returns from the previous verse in exactly the same metrical position, which makes the two verses sound like a matched pair even though one is about the army and the other about the princes. Keep the o long and let the dy be heard as two consonants.

On what to hold while chanting: this is the verse of the child. The tradition treats Bālā's mantra as the beginner's mantra, and there is an obvious lesson in the fact that the first thing the beginner is given is the figure who insisted on going into the hardest fight before she was ready and won it. It is also, plainly, a verse about a mother watching her daughter do something dangerous, and it does not ask to be read as anything else.

030.subtitle: A glance between them, and a son

commentary.meaning: The two halves of this verse have almost nothing in common, and the join between them is the most abrupt in the whole battle sequence. First the second brother falls: Vārāhī takes the life-breath out of Viśukra, and the strength she shows in doing it makes the goddess rejoice — the fourth and last of the names of watching. Then, with no transition at all, the register changes. Lalitā turns and looks at her husband's face; something passes between them; and out of that look the elephant-headed lord comes into existence. The verse says nothing about why he was needed, because the next verse will say it. What this name records is only the mechanism, and the mechanism is the point: no womb, no gestation, no austerity, no fire. The remover of obstacles was produced by a married couple glancing at one another in the middle of a war.
commentary.history:
Viśukra and Viṣaṅga were made, in the purāṇa's telling, out of the remainder of the same ash from which Bhaṇḍa himself was shaped, so all three of the enemy's commanders are the residue of the burnt god of desire. Vārāhī fights the second of them with a plough and a pestle — Balarāma's implements, farm tools used as clubs — and the name given to her act is prāṇaharaṇa, the carrying off of the breath. It is a precise word rather than a poetic one. She does not cut him down; she removes the vital air, which is what the tradition understands death to be.

The second half of the verse belongs to a different chapter of the story and, oddly, to an earlier one. Bhaṇḍa, watching his forces melt, had asked his brother what could be done, and Viśukra, who was the family's specialist in magic, proposed a device. Working under cover of darkness and hidden by māyā, he went up to the wall of fire, inscribed on a stone slab an eight-angled figure with eight tridents and eight guardian deities headed by Alasā, and threw it over into the enclosure. The slab was called Jayavighna, the obstruction of victory. Its effect on the army was immediate and is described symptom by symptom in the next verse's note. Mantriṇī and Daṇḍanāthā came to report that the śaktis would not fight.

What Lalitā did then is the whole of the second name. She looked at Kāmeśvara's face and smiled, showing a line of very red teeth, and from the meeting of that smile with that face there arose a god with an elephant's face, ruddy as the dawn, ten-armed, holding mace, trident, conch, lotus and tusk on one side and citron, bow, discus, a sheaf of grain and a jewelled pot in his trunk on the other, wearing red silk, three-eyed, with the crescent on his crown, his consort against his body and rut running from his temples. That is Mahāgaṇapati, the form of Gaṇeśa specific to this tradition, and the twenty-eight-syllable mantra addressed to him is very often the first mantra a Śrīvidyā student receives.

The verb the stotra uses for what she did to him is kalpita. Monier-Williams gives the range: formed, fabricated, contrived, invented, imagined. It is not the word for begetting. It is close to the vibhāvaye of the second meditation verse, where the reciter is told to bring the goddess into being by imagining her. Applied to Gaṇeśa the word says that he was thought up on the spot, in an emergency, by two people looking at each other — and that thinking him up was sufficient to produce him with ten arms and a wife.

One discrepancy is worth flagging because a careful reader will hit it. In the narrative chapters this episode comes before the deaths of Viśukra and Viṣaṅga: Gaṇeśa breaks the slab, comes out of the fire-fort with his own troops, and fights Viśukra, who runs; only later do Mantriṇī and Daṇḍanāthā kill the two brothers. The stotra reverses the order, putting both brothers in names 75 and 76 and Gaṇeśa in 77 and 78. It has grouped the material by category — the brothers together, the Gaṇeśa episode together — rather than following the days of the battle. Combined with the swapping of the two brothers' killers noted in the previous verse, this is good evidence that the hymn was composed against the story rather than out of it, by someone summarising from memory a narrative he expected his hearers to know better than he did.
commentary.practice:
This verse is the place to learn the rule that governs half the retroflex nasals in the stotra. In the first line you have prāṇa and haraṇa, and in both of them the n has become a retroflex ṇ. Neither is arbitrary. When an r or an ṛ or an ṣ has occurred earlier in the same word, a following n is pulled back into the retroflex position, even across intervening vowels and certain consonants. The pra of prāṇa does it; the ha-ra of haraṇa does it. Once you have the rule you will see it everywhere in this batch — varṣiṇī, dhāriṇī, svarūpiṇī, nirīkṣaṇa, and the aruṇa and karuṇā that run through the whole hymn — and you will also see where it does not apply, as in nanditā and mantriṇī, whose ṇ has a different cause.

The drill of the verse, though, is the pair of names Viśukra and Viṣaṅga. Viṣaṅga, in the line just past, has a retroflex ṣ: tongue-tip curled back. Viśukra, here, has a palatal ś: the tongue-body flat against the hard palate, the same position as the y in "yes". The two demons are separated in sound by one sibilant moved a single place forward in the mouth, and most learners collapse both into an English "sh". Say vi-ṣaṅ-ga, vi-śu-kra, back and forth. Then note that the kra of Viśukra is a plain unaspirated k with an r inside the same release, and that the u before it is short.

Vārāhī and vīrya want long vowels held to their full value: vā-rā-hī is three long syllables in a row, and vī-rya begins with a long ī and ends in a cluster of r and y that has to be got through without inserting a vowel between them. Vīr-ya, not vī-ri-ya.

The second line has one sandhi and one long compound. Kāmeśvara plus mukha plus āloka gives kāmeśvaramukhāloka, with the a of mukha and the ā of āloka merged into a single long ā — the seam falls in the middle of a written mātrā and cannot be heard, so the reader supplies it. After that the line runs kalpita-śrī-gaṇeśvarā with an lp cluster in the middle and the retroflex ṇ of gaṇa near the end. The natural breath is after -āloka, which is also the correct joint in the compound: everything before it is the glance, everything after it is what the glance made.

One last observation about sound and sense together. This verse ends the run of four names in which she is grammatically acted upon — harṣitā, samutsukā, nanditā, toṣitā, nanditā again — and the second name here is the first in the sequence where she is the one doing something, even if what she does is only look. From the next verse onward the participles turn active. The change in the grammar is the change in the plot.

On what to hold: the tradition's instruction here is unusually concrete, because Mahāgaṇapati is worshipped before Lalitā in every ritual sequence of this school. If you begin a recitation with a remembrance of Gaṇeśa, as most reciters do, this is the verse that tells you why he is there and what he was for.

031.subtitle: The engine of obstruction, and the answering rain

commentary.meaning: The first name finishes the episode the last verse began. The great Gaṇeśa split the obstruction-engine open, and she was overjoyed — praharṣitā, with the intensifying prefix, the strongest of the words for delight in this whole stretch and the last of them. Then the poem changes hands. From the second name onward the goddess fights. Bhaṇḍāsura, chief of demons, is loosing weapon after weapon and she is answering each with a shower of counter-missiles: pratyastra, the missile hurled back, the specific term for a weapon released to cancel another. The name ends in a present participle, varṣiṇī, raining, so the exchange does not conclude while you are saying it — it is still going on. Four verses of watching other people fight are over, and the last three names of the war are all hers.
commentary.history:
What Viśukra had thrown into the fire-fort was a stone slab a couple of krośas across, inscribed with an eight-angled figure and eight tridents, with eight deities stationed on it and Alasā, Sloth, at their head. Its name was Jayavighna, the obstruction of victory. What it produced in the army is set out as a list of eight, and the list is the most transparently allegorical thing in the entire war: sloth, meanness of spirit, wretchedness, sleep, unmanliness, forgetfulness, heedlessness and torpor. These are not the ways an army loses a battle. They are the ways a practice collapses. The śaktis stopped fighting, sat down, and began saying to one another that they were not sure the goddess was worth following.

The cure is equally pointed. Nothing is done to the enemy. The problem is inside the enclosure, so the newly made Gaṇeśa goes into the enclosure and looks for it, moving about within the wall of fire until he finds where the slab has been hidden; then he pounds it to powder with his tusks, destroys the deities posted on it, and throws the dust away on the wind. The morale returns at once, and the tradition takes his boon — that he shall be worshipped before all other gods, in every undertaking — to date from this service. That is why, in a school whose deity is Lalitā, the first invocation in every ritual is to her elephant-headed son.

The second name moves into the vocabulary of epic warfare, and the distinction it turns on is worth having. Śastra is a weapon held in the hand; astra is a missile discharged by mantra, a weapon that is really a formula. Every astra in the epic tradition has a counter, and a duel between two masters is conducted as an exchange of named missiles, each one neutralised by the correct answer. Pratyastra is that answer. The Lalitopākhyāna gives the whole exchange as a table: Bhaṇḍa releases a weapon that produces a particular kind of enemy, and she releases the deity who historically dealt with that kind. He brings back Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Raktabīja and the old demons of the Devī Māhātmya; she laughs, and the goddesses of that text come out of the laugh and kill them again. He brings back others; she answers. The pattern will produce, in the next verse, the most spectacular of the answers.

There is a joke buried in the arrangement, and it is a Sanskrit joke about grammar rather than a comic one. For eight names the goddess has been the object of other people's verbs: gladdened, made eager, delighted, satisfied, overjoyed. Every one of those participles is passive or causative. The moment she starts fighting, the grammar turns: varṣiṇī is an active participle in the feminine, she who rains, formed on the same root as the śaravarṣa, the rain of arrows, that is the oldest cliché in Indian battle poetry. The stotra has spent five verses telling you that she watches, and it announces her entry into the fight by changing a suffix.

One further point about the obstruction-engine that is easy to miss. The thing Viśukra inscribed was a yantra — a diagram, with angles and enclosures and deities set at the points. It is, in other words, the same kind of object as the Śrīcakra she is riding. The war has a diagram on each side, and the difference between them is not their form but what they are for.
commentary.practice:
The consonant work in this verse is heavy and it repays being taken slowly. Start with vighnayantra, which contains two clusters most learners flatten. Ghn is an aspirated guttural g running straight into a dental n, with the aspiration audible in between; ntr is dental n, dental t and r in a single release. Say vi-ghna-yan-tra. Then nirbhinna, which has rbh — an r followed by an aspirated b — and then a genuinely doubled nn that must be held long enough to hear as two. Then praharṣitā: pr at the front, and rṣ in the middle, where the r has pulled the sibilant back into the retroflex position, exactly as in harṣitā three verses ago.

The second line is a str exercise. Śastra, pratyastra: three clusters built on str in the space of eight syllables, and each one preceded by something different. Śastra opens with the palatal ś and then has a dental s inside the str. Pratyastra has pr, then ty, then str. The temptation is to let all of them turn into a single mushy sound. Take the line at half speed as bha-ṇḍā-su-ren-dra-nir-muk-ta | śa-stra-pra-tyas-tra-var-ṣi-ṇī and rebuild it.

Bhaṇḍāsurendra is three words fused: bhaṇḍa, asura, indra. Bhaṇḍa plus asura merges two a-sounds into one long ā, and asura plus indra merges an a and an i into a single e. Two seams, and in the Devanagari each shows as one vowel sign with nothing to indicate that a word has ended inside it. Learning to see भण्डासुरेन्द्र as three names rather than one is the same skill as learning to see क्रोधाकाराङ्कुश as four words, and it is the single most useful reading skill this text demands.

Nirmukta gives rm followed by kt, four consonants in a row across two syllables with only a short u between them. And varṣiṇī ends the verse with rṣ and then the retroflex ṇ produced by the same r — one letter causing two retroflexions in three syllables.

A metrical detail: this is the first verse in some while whose second name is an ī-stem rather than an ā-stem, so the line ends on a long ī instead of a long ā. After eight consecutive names closing on -ā the change is genuinely audible, and it happens to fall on precisely the name where she stops being the recipient of other people's valour and starts fighting. Let the vowel be heard.

As for what to hold in mind while chanting: the eight afflictions the engine produced are a fair description of what actually stops a daily practice, and the remedy in the story is not more effort but the removal of something that had been planted and hidden. It is a verse about looking for the obstruction rather than pushing harder against it.

032.subtitle: Ten descents out of her fingernails

commentary.meaning: The exchange of missiles reaches its height in the first name and the war effectively ends in the second. Bhaṇḍa's last resort has been to bring back the dead: a weapon that restores the great demons of earlier ages, the ones Viṣṇu had already dealt with once. Her answer is the most extravagant image in the hymn. From the nails on the fingers of her hand the ten descents of Nārāyaṇa come out, one for each returning enemy, and each of them kills again what it killed before. Then the second name clears the field. She looses the great Pāśupata, Śiva's own weapon and the most dangerous object in Sanskrit literature, and its fire leaves nothing at all of the demon soldiery. Between the two names the signature powers of both the other great gods have been spent. The stotra never says that she outranks them. It simply uses their equipment and moves on.
commentary.history:
The Lalitopākhyāna sets out this part of the battle as a table, weapon against counter-weapon, and it is worth having the table because the stotra reduces the whole of it to one word, daśākṛti, the ten forms. Bhaṇḍa releases the missile that produces the demon who stole the Vedas, and she answers with the fish. He sends the ocean-weapon, and the tortoise comes up to carry the śaktis on its back. He restores Hiraṇyākṣa, and the boar kills him again; Hiraṇyakaśipu, and the man-lion tears him apart; Bali, and the dwarf appears; Sahasrārjuna, and Paraśurāma; Rāvaṇa, and Rāma with his bow; a swarm of demons born as kings, and the fourfold Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha; the Kali missile, and Kalki.

That list is not the one on the calendars. This text's ten do not include the Buddha, they represent Kṛṣṇa by the four-fold emanation of the Pāñcarātra theology rather than by Kṛṣṇa himself, and they close with a form answering great delusion rather than with a familiar name. The set of ten was still settling when this material was composed, and here it has been arranged not by chronology but by function: each descent is defined by the enemy it exists to cancel. That is worth knowing before deciding what the stotra means by ten forms.

The detail about the fingernails is not an ornament either. Narasiṃha killed Hiraṇyakaśipu with his claws, because the demon's boon had ruled out every weapon; the avatāra of the nails is himself an avatāra about nails. This stotra has also been to her nails before. At name 44 the light coming off her toenails was said to burn away the darkness in those who bow to her — the hymn's foot-to-crown description ended there, and the same body-part now produces armed gods. A reader who has been chanting from the beginning will hear the echo.

The Pāśupata weapon in the second name carries an even heavier freight. In the Mahābhārata it is Śiva's supreme missile, obtained by Arjuna after a wrestling match with the god disguised as a mountain hunter, and it is given with an explicit warning: never to be discharged at an ordinary human being, because if released at a lesser target it would burn the world. That is exactly what she does with it. She uses the weapon that must not be used on lesser beings on the whole of the demon rank and file at once, and the name for the result is nirdagdha — burnt out, consumed, nothing left. It is the same participle the next verse will use for the destruction of the city.

The theological move here is the one the stotra has been making since its second verse, and it is worth naming because this is its largest instance. In verses two and three the bow, the arrows, the noose and the goad — the equipment of the god of desire — turned out to be hers. Here the ten bodies of Viṣṇu come off her hands like sparks and the ultimate weapon of Śiva is one of her arrows. The hymn does not argue for her supremacy. It demonstrates it by inventory.
commentary.practice:
The verse begins with a cluster most learners have not met yet. Karāṅguli has ṅg, the guttural nasal made at exactly the point where the g that follows it is made, so the tongue never travels between them; it is the same sound as in English "finger", which is a useful accident since aṅguli means finger. Say ka-rāṅ-gu-li with the ṅ closed and the g released.

Then a sandhi that the writing hides. Nakha plus utpanna gives nakhotpanna: a short a and a short u have fused into a single o, and the word-boundary has vanished. Inside the result you get tp, an unaspirated t running straight into a p, and then a doubled nn that has to be held. Na-kho-tpan-na.

The first name ends in a visarga, which is the first thing this verse asks you to do that the last six did not. Daśākṛtiḥ is an i-stem, so its nominative singular is -tiḥ and not -tā, and after nine consecutive names closing on a long ā the change is very audible. The visarga itself is a voiceless breath that carries a faint echo of the vowel before it — most southern reciters will give you a light ihi at the end of daśākṛtiḥ, and that is the traditional realisation, not an error.

Nirdagdha in the second line is the hardest cluster in the verse: a voiced g running directly into the voiced aspirate dh, with no vowel between them and the aspiration audible on the dh alone. Nir-dag-dha. It occurs again in the very next verse in the same position, so the practice carries over.

The second line is also a chain of three sandhi seams inside one word. Mahā plus pāśupata plus astra plus agni yields mahāpāśupatāstrāgni: pata and astra merge their a and ā into one long ā, and astra and agni do the same again a syllable later. Five long ā's in eight syllables, and none of the four original word-boundaries visible. Say it slowly as mahā-pāśupata-astra-agni before you say it as written, and the sense will stay attached to the sound.

One pleasant thing about the sibilants here. This verse has no retroflex ṣ at all, which is unusual for this stretch of the hymn. What it has is the palatal ś twice, in daśa and in pāśupata, against plain dental s in asura and sainika. After ten verses of curling the tongue back this is a rest, and it is worth noticing the relief as information: the poet has given you a line your tongue can lie flat for.

On what to hold while chanting: the image is very physical and should be allowed to be. Ten armed gods come out of the ends of her fingers, at the exact place where a hand stops being a hand. If the ten descents have ever felt like a doctrinal list to be recited, this verse puts them back where the tradition wants them, which is at the edge of a body.

033.subtitle: The empty city burned to nothing

commentary.meaning: The war ends in the first name and the hymn's whole attention changes in the second. The weapon named after her husband — Kāmeśvara, the lord of desire — burns Śūnyaka together with Bhaṇḍāsura inside it, and the compound does not trouble to separate the city from the man: sa-bhaṇḍāsura-śūnyaka, the empty place with the demon in it, is one object and it is consumed at one stroke. Then the sky fills with gratitude. Brahmā, Upendra, Mahendra and the gods behind them praise her vaibhava, the sheer extent of her power. The order is deliberate. The stotra has not allowed anyone to praise her until the thing she was raised to do is done, and the very first verse said what she was raised for: devakāryasamudyatā, risen out of the fire already braced for the gods' errand. Eighty-two names later, the errand is discharged.
commentary.history:
Bhaṇḍāsura could not simply be fought, and the reason is in his boon. When Brahmā granted him his powers the demon asked, among other things, that half the strength of any adversary who faced him should pass over into his own — which makes ordinary combat not merely difficult but self-defeating, since the harder you strike the stronger he gets. That is why the campaign is settled by a missile rather than by a duel, and why the missile has to be one that is not, in any straightforward sense, an opponent.

The Kāmeśvara weapon closes the largest circle in the whole story. Śiva burnt Kāma to ash with the fire of his eye; someone gathered the ash and shaped a figure from it; Brahmā's exclamation of astonishment gave the figure its name; the figure made the three worlds unliveable; the gods went into their own sacrificial fire; she came up out of it; and now she destroys him with a weapon named for Śiva in his aspect as the lord of desire. The thing made from the ashes of desire is destroyed by desire's own arm. The next verse will complete the circle by bringing Kāma himself back to life, so the whole of the Lalitā narrative sits inside the interval between the burning of the love-god and his restoration.

Śūnyaka is a name to sit with. It is simply the word śūnya, empty, with a suffix, and Monier-Williams gives it as empty, void, and as the absence or lack of something. The demon's capital is called the Empty Place, and the weapon reduces it to precisely what it was already named. Some accounts of the story call the city Śoṇitapura instead, the city of blood, but the reading in this hymn is śūnyaka and the pun is too good to be accidental. What was made out of ashes returns to ashes and what was called empty becomes empty; the stotra records both in one sixteen-syllable word and does not comment.

The second name gives the three highest gods in a single compound and it is worth taking them apart. Brahman is the creator. Upendra is Viṣṇu — the name means Indra's younger brother, and it belongs to him as Vāmana, born to Aditi after Indra was already established. Mahendra is Indra himself, the great Indra, king of the gods and the one with the actual grievance. So the compound runs creator, preserver, sovereign, and the -ādi at the end sweeps in everyone else. The hymn has been keeping a strict order of precedence throughout the battle — Mantriṇī beside her, Daṇḍanāthā in front, the Nityās on the field — and it observes it here too, at the point where the whole pantheon lines up to say thank you.

The narrative is a little less decorous than the hymn. In the purāṇa the gods do praise her at length, and then, in the same breath, ask her for something else: Bhaṇḍa is dead, they say, but his friend Tāraka is still alive, and to kill Tāraka Śiva must have a son, and for Śiva to have a son the god of love must be alive again, and he is currently ash. The great hymn of praise turns out to be a preamble to a request. That is the business of the next verse.

One small textual note for anyone comparing editions. Some print sabhaṇḍāsura with a short first vowel, some sabhāṇḍāsura with a long one, and the two spellings are found in different manuscript traditions of both the name and the surrounding narrative. Nothing in the sense turns on it, but if two printed books in front of you disagree, this is why.
commentary.practice:
This verse contains the best sandhi exercise in the whole batch, and it is the second name. Brahmopendramahendrādi is four words fused into one: brahman, upendra, mahendra, ādi. Brahma plus upendra has merged a short a and a short u into a single o. Mahā plus indra has merged a long ā and a short i into a single e — and that merger happened long ago, inside the name Mahendra itself, which is why it is easy to miss. Then mahendra plus ādi merges a and ā into one long ā. Three seams, three single written vowels, and no visual trace of where the words stopped. Take the compound apart on paper once and it will stay apart in your ear.

Nirdagdha returns from the previous verse in the same metrical position. Voiced g into voiced aspirated dh, no vowel between, aspiration on the second consonant only. Two verses running with the same cluster in the same place is the stotra offering you a drill; take it.

The sa- at the head of sabhaṇḍāsura is not part of the demon's name. It is the ordinary Sanskrit prefix meaning along with, the same syllable as in the sakuṅkuma and saśara of the fourth meditation verse, and it governs everything after it: the city, along with the demon. Keeping it separate in your mind keeps the compound from turning into an undifferentiated string.

Saṃstuta puts an anusvāra directly before a sibilant. Before s, ś or ṣ the anusvāra has nothing to assimilate to, so it stays a pure nasal hum with the mouth still open — not an n, not an m, just voice through the nose while the tongue gets ready for the s. Saṃ-stu-ta. The same thing happens in saṃsthitā in verse forty.

Now a small pleasure. Read the second line aloud and notice what is missing: brahmopendramahendrādidevasaṃstutavaibhavā has no retroflex consonant in it at all, and no conjunct harder than st. After eight verses of ṇḍ and kṣ and ṣṭ and gdh, the line where the gods sing is the one line your tongue can take flat. Whether the Vāgdevatās did that on purpose is unknowable; that the effect is there is not.

The two diphthongs are worth holding to their full length: the ai of vaibhavā and the e of -pendra- and -hendra-, which in Sanskrit are always long, however short the syllable feels.

On what to hold: many reciters treat this verse as the end of a section and take a fuller breath after it, because the battle finishes here and the next verse turns to the mantra. If you are chanting the hymn in parts over several days, this is a natural place to stop. It is also worth noticing what the hymn does not do at this point. There is no gloating, no description of the enemy's remains, and no account of the victory celebration — one line for the destruction, one line for the praise, and then the subject changes.

034.subtitle: The herb that brought desire back

commentary.meaning: The last act of the war and the first move of an entirely new section, side by side in one verse. The gods, having praised her, now ask: Kāma is still ash, and without Kāma there will be no marriage, no son, and no one to kill Tāraka. She looks at Rati with compassion and the love-god is reborn from that glance. The name for her here is not saviour or restorer but sañjīvana-auṣadhi, the life-restoring herb — the plant of the epics that revives the dead — for the one whom the fire of Hara's eye had burnt. Then the story simply stops. The second name says that her face is a lotus, and that this lotus is the one visible form of the first cluster of syllables in her mantra. With that the hymn changes its whole procedure: for the next two verses her body will be described as the fifteen-syllabled mantra written out in flesh.
commentary.history:
It is worth stopping at this point to see how large a detour has just closed. The chain begins with Tārakāsura, who held a boon that only a son of Śiva could kill him. Śiva was in mourning and in meditation and would not marry, so the gods sent Kāma to disturb him; Śiva opened his third eye and burnt him to ash; the ash was gathered and shaped into a figure, which became Bhaṇḍāsura and turned out to be a far worse problem than the one the gods had been trying to solve. The whole Lalitā narrative — her rising from the fire, her city, her army, the four days of battle — is an interpolated emergency inside the plot of the Kumārasambhava, and this verse is where the interpolation is closed and the original story allowed to resume. Kāma is revived, goes back to work on Śiva, this time succeeds, and Skanda is born and kills Tāraka. The purāṇa says so explicitly a few verses after the passage this name is drawn from.

The scene itself is domestic rather than cosmic. The gods bring Rati forward. She is described as a widow with her hair uncombed, which is the standard sign, and their argument to the goddess is not theological — they say that this woman is wretched, and that if the goddess reunites her with her husband she will be blessed. Lalitā looks at her, is moved, and out of the sidelong glance that follows Manmatha is reborn: better-looking than before, with a smiling face, only two arms this time, his bow and arrows made of flowers. He delights his wife with a look, the same way he was made.

The metaphor chosen for her is precise in a way that a general word like saviour would not be. Sañjīvanī is the herb of the Rāmāyaṇa, the one Hanumān goes to the mountain to fetch and brings back with the mountain attached because he cannot tell which plant it is. There is a second resonance: the demons' own preceptor Śukra was famous for possessing the mṛtasañjīvanī, the knowledge that raises the dead, and used it to keep resurrecting his side's casualties. The stotra calls the goddess not the person who administers the remedy but the remedy itself — the herb, not the physician. That is the same grammatical habit that made the noose desire's own form in verse two: she is not described as doing the thing, she is described as being the substance by which the thing is done.

The second name opens the mantra section and needs a word of orientation. The root mantra of this school has fifteen syllables and falls into three groups, called kūṭas — the word means a peak or summit, and by extension a heap or cluster, so the mantra has three summits. The first is the vāgbhava, that which arises as speech; the second the middle or kāmarāja cluster; the third the śakti cluster. Each of the three ends in the same syllable, which the tradition calls the hṛllekhā. The syllables themselves are given at initiation and are not printed here, but the Saundaryalaharī verse quoted below encodes them, letter by letter, in a way that has been decoded in print for a very long time — and that verse is itself the best evidence of how old and how stable the arrangement is.

What this name does with that structure is to map it onto her body. The vāgbhava cluster is her face. It is the cluster of speech, and the face is where speech comes from; and if you have read the frame narrative you will remember that the hymn you are reciting was composed by the goddesses of speech at her command. The next verse will take the middle cluster down to the waist and the third below it. The hymn is about to say that her body is not merely described by the mantra but is the mantra, in the plainest possible sense: three groups of syllables, three regions of a body, no remainder.
commentary.practice:
Two visarga-final names in three verses, and this is the second: auṣadhiḥ. The word packs four separate difficulties into four syllables — the diphthong au, which is long and must not collapse into a plain o; the retroflex ṣ; the aspirated dh, which is d with an audible puff and not the sound in English "the"; and the closing visarga, that light voiceless breath echoing the preceding i. Say au-ṣa-dhiḥ slowly four times.

Before it comes sañjīvana, with ñj — a palatal nasal followed by a palatal j. Because both are made at the same place the tongue does not move at all between them; the nasal simply stops and the voice comes out through the mouth. And before that, sandagdha: a dental nd, then the gdh you have now met three verses running.

Haranetrāgni is a straightforward vowel merger — netra plus agni, a and a into one long ā — but it is worth reconstructing because it keeps the picture in view. Hara's eye, the eye's fire: three words in five syllables.

The second line contains the two most instructive consonant sandhis in the batch, and both are visible in the writing. Śrīmat plus vāgbhava has become śrīmadvāgbhava, because a final unvoiced t before the voiced v is itself voiced to d — the same change you met in cidagni in the very first verse. And vāgbhava is itself vāc plus bhava: the palatal c of vāc, speech, becomes a guttural g before the voiced aspirate bh. So the word for the speech-cluster has had its own first consonant altered by the second half of the compound, and the writing preserves the evidence. When you chant śrīmadvāgbhava you are saying śrīmat vāc bhava with two joints greased.

Then kūṭaika, which is kūṭa plus eka. A short a followed by e does not merge into e; it strengthens to ai. This is the vṛddhi merger, less common than the ones that give ā and o and e, and it is about to recur three more times in the next two verses — kūṭaikatā, mūlādhāraika, kulāmṛtaika. Learn its signature now: whenever you see an ai in the middle of a compound in this hymn, suspect a following eka or ekatā.

The rest of the second line is retroflex work. Kūṭa has the retroflex ṭ, and mukhapaṅkajā ends on ṅk, the guttural nasal again, made at the point of the k. Between them svarūpa gives you a plain dental s and a rolled r.

A point of rhythm: the caesura in the second line falls after -eka-, at the eighth syllable, which is also where the compound divides between the mantra-cluster and the body-part. For once the metrical joint and the grammatical joint coincide. Breathe there.

On what to hold: this verse is the seam of the whole hymn. The first name looks back at everything that has happened since the goddess rose from the fire; the second looks forward into the mantra, the body, the six centres and the coiled power, which is what the rest of this stretch of the stotra is about. Chanted attentively it should feel like a door.

035.subtitle: A body divided into three mantras

commentary.meaning: The scheme opened at the end of the last verse is now carried through the rest of her. Everything from below the throat down to the waist is the middle cluster of the mantra, taken on as a form; everything from the waist downward has come into oneness with the third cluster, and she bears it. Two names, two regions, and with the face already assigned there is nothing of her left over. What repays notice is that the two names use different grammars for what is the same claim. In the first she is svarūpiṇī, one who has that as her own form — the identification is simple being. In the second the region has attained ekatā, oneness, with the cluster, and she is described as its dhāriṇī, the one who carries it. So she both is the mantra and holds it, and the hymn does not choose between the two.
commentary.history:
This is the second head-to-foot description of the goddess in the stotra, and it is worth putting the two side by side. The first ran from name 13 to name 51 and was made of visible things: four kinds of blossom in her hair, a ruby diadem, the half-moon of her forehead, musk on the brow, and so on down to the toenails whose light dispels darkness. It took thirty-nine names. The second takes three, occupies two verses, and is made entirely of sound. It is the same body twice, once painted and once spelled.

The division points are the throat and the waist, and they are chosen rather than obvious. Kaṇṭhādhaḥ means below the throat, kaṭiparyanta means as far as the hips, so the middle cluster occupies the trunk — the chest, the heart, the breath — while the first cluster had the head and the third has everything from the waist down. In yogic anatomy those two lines matter independently: the throat is a junction, the waist is where the lower centres begin. Here they are being used as the seams of a garment made of syllables.

The fifteen-syllabled mantra falls into three groups of five, six and four, and the tradition calls each a kūṭa, a peak or summit; each ends in the same syllable, the hṛllekhā. The first is the vāgbhava, of speech; the second is the middle cluster, also called the kāmarāja, the sovereignty of desire; the third is the śakti cluster. Beyond that, a great many correspondences have been proposed and are transmitted with varying confidence — the three to the sun, moon and fire; to waking, dream and deep sleep; to will, knowledge and action; to the three great gods. These are the tradition's own reflections rather than statements in the text, and it is worth holding them lightly. What the text itself asserts is narrower and stranger: three groups of syllables, three regions of a body, and an equals sign.

One of the several traditional explanations of her name Tripurasundarī, the beauty of the three cities, takes the three cities to be exactly these three clusters. Others take them as the three worlds, the three states of consciousness, or the three cities Śiva burnt. All of these circulate, and the tradition has never been embarrassed by having four incompatible etymologies for its central name. But the reading that makes the three cities the three kūṭas is the one these two verses support, because they have just built her out of three parts and called each part a mantra.

The underlying operation — take a body, divide it, and equate each part with a member of some other ordered set — is very old in India. The Ṛgvedic hymn of the cosmic person does it, mapping mouth, arms, thighs and feet onto the divisions of society; the Upaniṣads do it with the sheaths; the tantric traditions do it with mantras, and the technical name for the result is the mantra-body. What distinguishes the version here is the direction of the identification. In the older cases the body is the source and the categories are read out of it. Here the mantra is the source, and the body is what the mantra looks like when it is seen rather than heard.

There is a practical consequence, and it is the reason this material is placed just after the nyāsa in every ritual manual. If the three clusters are three regions of her body, then placing those clusters on the corresponding regions of one's own body — which is precisely what the nyāsa preceding this stotra does — is not a symbolic act but a construction. The reciter assembles the goddess's body on his own before saying her names.
commentary.practice:
This verse contains the single best sandhi demonstration in the entire batch, and it is nearly invisible unless someone points it out. The word adhas, below, occurs twice — once in each line — and it appears in two completely different shapes.

In the first line, kaṇṭha plus adhas gives kaṇṭhādhaḥ, and because the next word begins with the unvoiced k of kaṭi, the final s has become a visarga and stayed there: कण्ठाधःकटि. That is a visarga sitting in the middle of a compound, which learners almost never expect. In the second line, kaṭi plus adhas plus bhāga gives kaṭyadhobhāga: the i of kaṭi has turned into y before the following vowel, exactly as in mantriṇyambā two verses ago, and then the final s of adhas, standing before the voiced bh, has turned the whole syllable into -o. कट्यधोभाग. Same word, two environments, two outcomes, both written out where you can see them. Say kaṇṭhādhaḥ and kaṭyadho one after the other and the rule for visarga before unvoiced and voiced consonants will stay learned.

The visarga in kaṇṭhādhaḥkaṭi also needs its own attention as a sound. Before a k, the traditional realisation is a light aspirate made far back in the throat — some grammarians give it its own name, jihvāmūlīya — and in ordinary recitation you will hear it as a short breath with a faint echo of the preceding a. Do not simply drop it; the syllable count depends on it being there.

Both names end in -ṇī, and both of those retroflex nasals are produced by the rule met in verse thirty: an r earlier in the word pulls a following n back. Svarūpiṇī has it from the r of rūpa, dhāriṇī from the r of dhāra. Two clean examples in two lines.

The vṛddhi merger promised in the last verse duly returns: śaktikūṭa plus ekatā has given śaktikūṭaikatā, a short a and an e strengthening into ai. Then ekatā plus āpanna merges two ā-sounds. Two seams inside one word again.

For clusters, the verse asks for ṇṭh at the very start — retroflex ṇ, retroflex aspirated ṭh, one gesture with a puff of breath at the end of it — then ry in paryanta, then dhy in madhya, then the sv of svarūpiṇī, which is a dental s followed by a v inside the same release and not a vowel between them. Kaṇṭhādhaḥ is worth ten repetitions on its own.

Rhythmically the two lines rhyme, both closing on -iṇī and -iṇī, and both are single sixteen-syllable names with the caesura falling inside a word. In the first line it lands after -paryanta-, which is a real joint in the compound; in the second it lands inside -kaṭyadho-, which is not. Take the breath at the line end.

On what to hold: chanting these two names is the only point in the hymn where you are asked to run your attention down the length of a body in a straight line, from the throat to the waist and then from the waist to the ground, and to hear the sound of it as you go. The nyāsa done before the recitation has already placed the same three groups on your own throat, trunk and hips. If you have done it, this verse is a description of where your hands have been.

036.subtitle: Made of the root mantra, sworn to the kula

commentary.meaning: Four names, two to a line, and for the first time since verse twenty-three the sixteen-syllable single name gives way to something shorter and quicker. The first two finish the argument of the last two verses and state it flatly: she does not stand for the root mantra, her very self is it, and her bodily frame is the three root clusters taken together. Then the second line changes subject without warning and puts down the word that will occupy the whole of the next verse. There is one taste she has, and it is the nectar of the kula; and she is the keeper of the kula's saṅketa — its private compact, its prearranged sign, the agreement its members hold among themselves. In half a verse the hymn has moved from the mantra to the community that transmits it, and it has done so by way of a word that means both a covenant and a lovers' rendezvous.
commentary.history:
Mūlamantra is a technical term: the root mantra of a deity, the one from which the ancillary formulas of a rite are derived. For this school it is the fifteen-syllabled mantra whose three clusters have just been mapped onto her body. What the first name adds is the suffix -ātmaka, which the dictionary glosses as having or consisting of the nature of. She is not the deity of the mantra, not the meaning of the mantra, not what the mantra is about. The mantra is what she consists of.

The second name says the same thing in a coarser register, and the choice of word is worth noticing. Kalevara is the ordinary word for a bodily frame — the physical carcass rather than the honorific vapus or the neutral śarīra — and in later usage it drifts toward meaning a corpse. To say that her kalevara is the three clusters is to make the identification physical and slightly blunt. This is characteristic of the hymn. It has just spent two verses on an elegant tripartite scheme, and it closes the argument with a word you might use of a body being carried out.

With the third name the hymn crosses into the vocabulary that will dominate the next verse, and kula is a word whose difficulty is worth facing squarely rather than glossing over. Monier-Williams gives it first as a herd or flock or swarm — a collection of like things — then as a race, family, community, tribe, caste, and then as the house that such a group lives in. In tantric usage it carries all of that and more: the assemblage of powers that make up the manifest world, the lineage of teachers and initiates through which a practice is transmitted, and, in the Kashmirian traditions, Śakti herself as against Śiva. Read the third name with the first sense and it says she relishes the nectar of the totality. Read it with the second and it says she relishes what the lineage possesses. Both are current and neither excludes the other.

Kulāmṛta, the nectar of the kula, is where the tradition's internal disagreement becomes visible for the first time in this hymn. One reading takes it as the flow of amṛta in the crown of the head — the flood the stotra will reach in three verses at name 106, sudhāsārābhivarṣiṇī. The other takes it as the ritual substances of the left-hand rite, of which wine is one. Commentators have gone both ways, and a good many have gone both ways at once, which is not evasion so much as house style: this is a tradition that likes a word to be doing two jobs. It is worth registering the ambiguity here rather than resolving it, because the next verse will name both parties to the argument by name.

Saṃketa in the last name is a similarly double word. The dictionary's first sense is an agreement or stipulation, its second is an assignation, specifically with a lover, and its third is a preconcerted sign or signal. All three are alive in this compound. The kula has a doctrine held under agreement, it has passwords and gestures by which its members recognise one another, and its central rite is a meeting. And she is its pālinī, its guardian: the one who keeps the secret, which in this tradition means the one who decides who is told.

That last point is not abstract. The frame narrative of this very hymn turns on it. Agastya asked for the thousand names and Hayagrīva refused, and when he finally gave them he said he was doing so because Agastya had asked twice and asked in devotion — the text calls it rahasya, secret, in so many words. The fifteen syllables themselves are still not printed in most editions of the ritual manuals and are given at initiation. Calling the goddess the guardian of the compact is the hymn's acknowledgement, in the middle of a public recitation, that the recitation is not the whole of what there is.
commentary.practice:
The first thing to notice about this verse is its rhythm, because it has changed. For eleven verses running each line has been a single sixteen-syllable name, and the caesura at the eighth syllable has fallen inside a word every time. Here each line is two names of eight syllables, and the caesura falls exactly at the join. For the first time in a long while you may take a real breath in the middle of a line. Mūlamantrātmikā, breath, mūlakūṭatrayakalevarā; kulāmṛtaikarasikā, breath, kulasaṅketapālinī. After twelve verses of holding, the release is very noticeable, and it is the reason this verse and the next are the two most commonly used in archanā, where each name is turned into a dative and given a flower.

The four names also alliterate at their heads in pairs: mūla, mūla, kula, kula. Two long ū's and then two short u's, in the same position, four times. Let that pattern carry the verse.

Mūlamantrātmikā has one sandhi and one cluster. Mantra plus ātmikā merges an a and an ā into one long ā; and ātmikā contains tm, a dental t immediately followed by m, which must be released as two consonants rather than collapsed. Āt-mi-kā.

Kulāmṛtaikarasikā has two seams and both are worth reconstructing. Kula plus amṛta merges two a-sounds into a long ā; then amṛta plus eka strengthens an a and an e into ai — the vṛddhi merger for the third time in three verses, and by now it should be recognisable on sight. There is also the syllabic ṛ of amṛta in the middle, which stays short.

Kulasaṅketapālinī gives you ṅk, the guttural nasal made at exactly the place of the k that follows, so the tongue does not travel. The same cluster appeared in mukhapaṅkajā two verses back. And the final ṇ of pālinī is one of the few in this batch that is not retroflex: there is no r or ṛ or ṣ earlier in the word to trigger the rule, so it stays a plain dental n. Compare it directly with svarūpiṇī and dhāriṇī in the previous verse, where the rule did apply. Pā-li-nī against dhā-ri-ṇī: the difference is audible and it is the rule made visible.

One more small thing. Kalevarā is easy to rush because it has no clusters and no long vowels until the end. Give the l and the v their full value and let the final ā take its length; the line needs the weight.

On what to hold: the verse turns, in the middle, from what she is made of to who is allowed to know. Chanting it aloud in a room is a mild paradox, and the tradition is aware of the paradox — the hymn is public and the mantra it is built out of is not. The traditional counsel is not to resolve that but to notice it: you are saying, out loud, the name of the one who keeps the thing you are not saying.
